opus-5.5.text:
I think in theoretical physics the postdoc stage is actually quite special, and the independence is much higher than people outside the field might imagine.

During a PhD you usually have an advisor, and even if they give you a lot of freedom, there is still a sense that you are working within their research program. You're learning their taste, their way of asking questions. When you become a postdoc in theoretical physics, especially at places like the big theory groups in the US, nobody really tells you what to do. You don't have a lab to maintain, you don't have experiments that need funding, you mainly need a pen, some paper, and maybe a computer. So in principle you can work on whatever you want, collaborate with whoever you want.

That freedom is both a gift and a test. The gift is that you can finally pursue questions you personally find deep. For me, things like quantum gravity, black holes, how information behaves in those systems, I could just follow my curiosity and talk to people I admired. The test is that there is no external structure forcing you to make progress. If you don't have your own judgment about which problems are worth working on, you can easily drift for a year or two. And the postdoc is short, usually two or three years, then you have to apply again. So you are very independent, but you are also under pressure to show that your independence produces something.

I'd say the postdoc is really where you find out whether you have your own research taste. In a PhD you can borrow your advisor's taste. As a postdoc you can't really borrow it anymore; you have to decide for yourself what is important. Some people thrive in that, some people find it quite lonely.

For me personally, that period was very valuable, but it also made me think more seriously about what kind of problems I want to spend my life on. Theoretical physics gives you a lot of intellectual freedom, but the feedback loop is very slow. You might work on something for years and still not know if it's connected to reality. That's partly why later I started to feel that I wanted to work on something where progress is faster and you can see the impact more directly, which eventually led me toward AI.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a postdoc can “work on whatever you want” and pursue questions they personally find deep.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses freedom and pressure but does not liken the position to philanthropy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the independence of a postdoc is one of the most misunderstood things about the position. On paper, a postdoc is the first time in your career where nobody is formally your advisor. You're not a student anymore, you don't have to pass exams, and in theoretical physics you often don't even have a group you're obligated to serve, because there's no lab, no equipment, no grant that requires you to produce a specific measurement. So in principle it's the most free you will ever be. You have maybe three years, a salary, an office, and the only thing anyone expects is that you think about interesting problems.

But in practice, that freedom is very constrained, and the constraint comes from the clock. Three years sounds long, but you have to start applying for faculty jobs in the second year, which means the work that will be judged has to be done in the first eighteen months or so. So the honest version of the question is: can you be independent in a way that also produces visible results in a year and a half? And that pushes people toward one of two failure modes. One is that you simply continue your PhD thesis, because that's the fastest way to generate papers, and then you arrive at the faculty market looking like an extension of your advisor. The other is that you take the freedom very seriously, switch to a completely new direction, and then have nothing to show when the applications are due.

My own view is that independence isn't really about which problem you choose, it's about whether you are the one deciding what counts as a good problem. During a PhD, your taste is largely borrowed from your advisor. The postdoc is when you have to develop your own taste, and that's a slower and more uncomfortable process than people admit. You can tell when someone has done it, because they start saying "I don't think that direction is interesting" about things that are currently fashionable, and they can explain why. That judgment is the real independence. The institutional independence, the fact that nobody is signing off on your work, is just the condition that makes it possible.

I'd also say that the best postdocs I've seen are not the ones who isolate themselves to prove they can work alone. They collaborate a lot, often more than during their PhD, but the collaborations are ones they initiated, around questions they chose. Independence and collaboration aren't opposites. Being the person who set the agenda in a joint project is much stronger evidence of maturity than being the single author on something small.

So I'd put it this way: the postdoc gives you independence as an opportunity, not as an outcome. Whether you actually become independent depends on whether you use those years to figure out what you think is important, and whether you're willing to accept some risk to the application timeline in order to do that. For me, that tradeoff was worth it, but I wouldn't pretend it's free.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a postdoc is, in principle, highly free, with no required lab or grant project, and describes choosing a new direction or deciding which problems matter.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare a postdoctoral position to philanthropy.

astra-6.text:
我觉得要区分两种独立性：一种是研究上的独立，另一种是职位和资源上的独立。理论物理的博士后，在研究上可以有相当大的自主性，比如自己提出问题、选择合作者，不一定所有工作都围绕某一位教授展开。当然，这也取决于具体的研究组、经费来源，以及双方对这个职位的期待。

但博士后毕竟是一个有期限的职位，你还要考虑下一份工作，需要成果，也需要同行认可。所以有选择课题的自由，并不意味着完全没有约束。有时候，求职的压力会让人倾向于做短期内更容易出结果的问题。

对我来说，更重要的独立性，是你能不能形成自己的判断：为什么这个问题值得做，什么样的结果才算真正推进了理解。这和你是不是独自完成一篇论文，不是同一回事。

r001.rationale: It says postdocs have freedom to choose research topics and can propose their own questions.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare a theoretical physics postdoctoral position to philanthropy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think independence has at least two meanings here. One is whether you can choose your own research questions; the other is whether you have the resources and security to pursue them. A postdoc might have considerable freedom in the first sense while still depending on a principal investigator for funding, recommendations, or the next position.

In theoretical physics, you can often develop an idea without a large experimental infrastructure, so there is room for intellectual independence. But that doesn’t mean independence happens automatically. If you’re constantly thinking about what will produce a paper quickly or help you get your next job, that shapes the questions you’re willing to ask.

So I would look less at the title and more at the actual arrangement: Can you start your own projects? Can you collaborate outside the group? Can you disagree with your advisor? Ideally, a postdoc gives you enough support to take risks while allowing you to develop your own scientific judgment.

r001.rationale: It says a postdoc may have considerable freedom to choose research questions, describing intellectual independence in theoretical physics.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a theoretical physics postdoctoral position to philanthropy.
